units.translation: There is hope that the end will come at night.
No hope of fear walks within my house.
prey, spoil
prey, spoil
And then I do not refuse to become prey for dogs and a feast for the birds of the land.
of myself
of myself
In no way being fearless of myself.
I will speak of my own grievous life.
Why then do I have these things to mock myself?
Seeing myself thus insulted.
I threw myself from this rugged rock.
to step in, to set foot upon, to trample
to step in
to set foot upon
to trample
You have entered upon this oracle with truth.
With these purple garments I am stepping on.
How cruelly the god has stepped upon the race of the Persians.
to throw in, to cast upon
to throw in, to cast upon
Having cast upon them, outside the walls, ruin that makes them throw away their shields.
And cast into the purple sea the dark-benched ruin.
Having thrown in an invading army.
Having thrown in an invading army.

a stepping in, entrance
Concerning that on which one treads
Let someone quickly loosen the sandal, the slave's stepping of the foot.
to set foot in, to frequent
to set foot in, to frequent
Frequent use of the verb concerning gods visiting places dear to them: see examples collected in the Thesaurus vol. 3 p. 808.
The island – which Pan, lover of the dance, frequents.

an invasion
Concerning the ramming of ships

θίς [a heap]: – and in the feminine gender for the heap in Aeschylus (fr. 335) “θινὸς ἐμβολὰς ἁλός” [the inroads of the sea upon the shore]. Since neither the meaning nor the gender is approved, Hermann conjectured θινὸς ἐμβολάδος [of the shore that is dashed against].
Overpowered by the rammings of ships.
They were struck by bronze-mouthed rammings (Stanley: by bronze-mouthed beaks).
A Greek ship began the ramming.
The ships destroyed them with utterly destructive rammings.

Middle form of the future
Hippocrates uses the Ionic future form ἐμέομαι [I will vomit].
And he falls back from the slaughter, vomiting.
Vomiting the clots of blood which you drew off from the murder.
He vomits (M: in my) the poison, not heavy upon his enemies.

a liquid medicine soaked into lint and inserted into wounds; metaphorically, something that clings
properly it is a liquid medicine, which, received on torn pieces of linen, is placed within ulcers and their cavities: see Thes. vol. 3 p. 845. Improperly
i.e. clinging. For Schuetz rightly restored ἄκος [a remedy] for ἑκάς [far away].
For these houses there is a remedy that clings, and not from others outside,
